web_reasoning: Web evidence confirms both names refer to the same Luxembourg Moselle producer. Search result [2] for A explicitly identifies 'Domaine Viticole Schumacher-Knepper' managed by Frank Schumacher and sister Martine since 2003. Search result [2] for B returns the identical wein.plus entry, confirming the same entity. Wine catalog overlap is substantial: both carry Wormeldange Koeppchen Riesling, Wintrange Felsberg variants, and Cremant lines from the same terroirs. 'Schumacher-Knepper' is the full historical/legal name; 'Schumacher' is the shortened brand form used on modern labels (per §11.6 label-form preference). Survivor: Schumacher (45 wines vs 17, more complete catalog).

Web search converges on single official entity 'Azienda Agricola Mazzi' / 'Roberto Mazzi' (robertomazzi.it) for both queries. Producer B 'Private Mazzi' is a private-label or secondary bottling variant of the same Mazzi family winery in Negrar, Valpolicella. Both wines are Amarone della Valpolicella from the same region/producer; 'Private' prefix indicates a custom-crush or retailer-exclusive line under the Mazzi brand (§11.4.c). Shared wine category (Amarone Classico) + identical location + single official website confirm same producer identity on label.

Web evidence converges decisively: both producer names resolve to the same official website (danzantewines.com) and the same corporate entity (Tenute di Toscana Distribuzione / Marchesi de' Frescobaldi ownership). The Italian business registry (fatturatoitalia.it) confirms 'La Capra Danzante' is located in Chiusi, Siena, Toscana — consistent with Danzante's Tuscan base. 'La Capra Danzante' is a historical or regional brand variant of 'Danzante' under unified ownership. The wine catalog divergence (Umbria Rosso vs. multi-region Pinot Grigio/Prosecco) reflects different product lines or vintages within the same producer portfolio, not separate wineries. Per §11.6, survivor name should be 'Danzante' (the form on current labels and official website).

Web evidence reveals both producer names resolve to the same official website (pierremeurgey.com) and the same Banville Wine Merchants producer page. The website describes a fourth-generation Burgundy winemaker named Pierre Meurgey producing from multiple communes including Clessé (Mâcon region) and broader Burgundy appellations. 'Meurgey Croses' appears to be a variant name or importer-bundled form of the same producer. The wine catalogs span both Côte d'Or (Pommard, Beaune, Pernand-Vergelesses) and Mâcon (Pouilly-Fuissé, Vire-Clesse, Mâcon) regions, consistent with a single multi-vineyard estate. §11.4.h (variant naming) + web convergence on single brand identity override the L1 geographic-separation reasoning.

Web search for both 'Pascal Jolivet' and 'Jolivet' converges on a single official website (pascaljolivet.com) and a single house identity ('House founded in 1987 - Pascal Jolivet'). Producer B's three wines are all labeled 'Domaine Jolivet, Saint-Joseph' — a distinct appellation from Pascal Jolivet's Sancerre/Pouilly Fumé focus, but the web evidence shows no separate 'Domaine Jolivet' entity or website. Per §11.4.e and §11.6, 'Domaine Jolivet' appears to be a second wine or estate line under the Pascal Jolivet umbrella rather than a distinct producer. The single official brand identity on the web (pascaljolivet.com) and the absence of a separate Domaine Jolivet web presence indicate these should MERGE, with 'Pascal Jolivet' as the survivor name (the form appearing on most labels and the official website).

Producer B 'Hospices de Beaune (Cecile Tremblay)' is a shipper/négociant variant of the canonical 'Hospices de Beaune' institution per §11.4.i. Web evidence confirms Hospices de Beaune is a single historic estate (founded 1443, steward Ludivine Griveau since 2015) that auctions cuvées to multiple négociants for bottling and distribution. Cecile Tremblay is a shipper/distributor name appended to the label, not a distinct brand identity. The single wine in B ('Corton Grand Cru, Les Renardes Cuvee Piece des Presidents') is a canonical Hospices de Beaune cuvée that appears in A's catalog. Merge B into A, recording 'Cecile Tremblay' as a shipper variant in producer_aliases.

Web evidence establishes that Vincent Marie and Marie et Vincent Tricot are the same producer operating under two distinct brand identities. The Zev Rovine Selections and ZRSWEST pages confirm 'Marie and Vincent Tricot' / 'Vincent and Marie Tricot' as the primary brand (established 2003, Auvergne, sulfur-free winemaking). The No Control website (vin-nocontrol.fr) and more-than-wine.com explicitly identify 'Vincent Marie – No Control' as the same vigneron in Volvic, Auvergne, producing natural wines. This is a case of one producer operating under two label brands (primary: Marie et Vincent Tricot; secondary: No Control) — per §11.2, distinct brand identities under shared ownership should be PARENT_CHILD; however, the evidence suggests No Control is a secondary/alternative label of the same entity rather than a separate legal brand. The minimal wine overlap (1 wine under No Control vs. 5 under Marie et Vincent Tricot) and the identical person-name core (Vincent Marie / Marie et Vincent) indicate a single continuous producer using two commercial names. Recommend MERGE with survivor 'Marie et Vincent Tricot' (primary label form on most wines) and alias 'No Control' recorded as `alias_type='secondary_label'`.

Web evidence converges on a single producer entity 'Terre al Piano' across multiple merchant platforms (Vivino, Vinello, Antonio's Wine). Search results for Producer A ('Terre Piano') return only 'Terre al Piano' products, indicating the shorter form is a variant or alias of the full brand name. Both producers are Italian, and the wine catalogs overlap (Montepulciano d'Abruzzo appears in both web results). The 'al' is a minor orthographic variant (common in Italian naming: 'Terre' = lands, 'al Piano' = at/on the plain). Per §11.1 and §11.4.h, accent/spelling variants of the same brand identity should MERGE; the survivor name should be 'Terre al Piano' (the form appearing on most current labels and merchant sites).

Web evidence converges on a single producer identity: Jancis Robinson lists 'Manuel Marinacci, Paja 2008 Barbaresco' as a wine under the single producer 'Manuel Marinacci'; a-mano import describes 'Barbaresco Paja' as Manuel's single-vineyard bottling ('The greatest example of noble wines. Manuel's number one'). 'Paja' is a vineyard designation within Manuel Marinacci's portfolio, not a separate producer. Both rows carry identical wine types (Barbaresco, Dolcetto d'Alba, Barbera d'Alba) from the same San Rocco Seno d'Elvio location. Producer B should be merged as a vineyard-specific variant under the unified 'Manuel Marinacci' brand identity per §11.6.

Web evidence converges on a single unified entity: 'Edmond de Rothschild Heritage' (EDRH) operates a portfolio of 7 domains across 500 hectares. Both producer names refer to the same Rothschild family wine operation — 'Barons Edmond Benjamin de Rothschild' and 'Baron Benjamin de Rothschild' are variant label forms of the same brand identity under EDRH stewardship. The Wine-Searcher result explicitly lists 'Barons Edmond & Benjamin de Rothschild' as a single producer entity for the Haut-Médoc wine. The prefix variation ('Barons' vs 'Baron') reflects label design choices, not distinct family branches — both trace to Benjamin de Rothschild's stewardship of the consolidated EDRH wine portfolio post-2004. Survivor name should be 'Barons Edmond Benjamin de Rothschild' (matches the Wine-Searcher canonical form and the actual wine label shown in A's catalog).

Web search for Producer B ('De La Coulerette') returns official château pages confirming 'Château de la Coulerette' in La Londe-les-Maures, Côtes de Provence. Producer A's wine 'Chateau Coulerette, Mademoiselle Tara' and Producer B's wine 'Chateau De La Coulerette, La Londe' both reference the same estate in the same appellation and commune. The web evidence establishes a single continuous brand identity ('Château de la Coulerette' / 'Château Coulerette') — the 'De La' prefix is a stylistic variant on the same label. Per §11.4.h (accent/diacritic variants) and §11.1 (spelling variants), these are the same producer. Survivor should be 'Château de la Coulerette' (the form appearing on official tourism/château websites).

Web evidence converges on a single Pomerol estate: both searches return the same thewinecellarinsider.com profile for 'Chateau Le Moulin' (result [1] for both A and B), and CellarTracker [2] explicitly lists 'Château Le Moulin Basileus' as the full formal name. The wine catalog (DirectChateau [3]) confirms 'Château Le Moulin Basileus' as the label brand. Producer A 'Moulin' is a short-form variant; Producer B 'Le Moulin Basileus' is the complete château name appearing on bottles. Per §11.1 (spelling/abbreviation variant) and §11.6 (label-form preference), the survivor should be 'Château Le Moulin Basileus' — the form that appears on actual labels today.

Web search for 'Altrevida' returns results exclusively for 'Atrevida' (Vivino, Wine Enthusiast, Firstleaf all converge on the same Mendoza winery). This strong convergence indicates 'Altrevida' is a typo or data-entry variant of 'Atrevida'. Both rows carry identical wine types (Malbec, Chardonnay) from the same Mendoza region with no distinguishing metadata. The trigram similarity (0.58) combined with web-search collapse to a single brand identity strongly supports MERGE under §11.1 (same normalized name, same country, same wine catalog pattern). Survivor: 'Atrevida' (appears on all merchant/review sites).

Web evidence converges on a single producer: all search results for both 'Behere Courtin' and 'Behere' resolve to 'Château Béhèré Courtin' (with accent variants). Wine-Searcher, Winestyle, and Wine Enthusiast all reference the same small Pauillac property (4.81 hectares, Cabernet/Merlot/Petit Verdot blend, located near Mouton Rothschild). The label identity is 'Château Béhèré Courtin'; Producer B's row ('Behere') is a short-form variant or import artifact. Single wine catalog overlap + unified web identity + accent/spelling normalization (Béhèré vs Behere) per §11.4.h. Survivor: 'Château Béhèré Courtin' (official label form with accents).

Web evidence converges on a single official website (tulbaghwine.co.za) for both search queries. Producer A's web results reference 'Tulbagh Mountain Vineyards' as a distinct property within the Tulbagh region, while Producer B's search returns the main 'Tulbagh Wine' homepage. The catalog overlap (both produce Syrah-based blends from Tulbagh region) combined with the unified web presence strongly suggests these are variant names for the same producer entity. Producer B ('Tulbagh') is likely the primary/umbrella brand name, with 'Tulbagh Mountain' as a sub-label or vineyard designation. §11.6 survivor rule: 'Tulbagh Wine' (or 'Tulbagh') should be the canonical name, with 'Tulbagh Mountain' recorded as an alias.

Web evidence converges: both 'Mary Taylor (Jean Marc Barthez)' and 'Barthez' refer to the same winemaker Jean-Marc Barthez and his cooperative in Monségur, Bordeaux. The Mary Taylor brand is the label identity (appearing on bottles), while Barthez is a shortened reference to the same producer. Wine catalogs overlap (both carry Bordeaux Rouge and Blanc from the same cooperative). Per §11.1 and §11.6, the survivor should be 'Mary Taylor (Jean Marc Barthez)' as it is the full brand form appearing on labels.

Web evidence confirms Niepoort Projectos is a distinct sub-brand under the Niepoort umbrella. Polaner Selections describes 'Niepoort Projectos' as Dirk [Niepoort]'s experimental/collaborative line ('make wines from around Europe at friends' wineries'), while the main Niepoort website (niepoort.pt) lists the core portfolio (Ports, Douro, Dão, Bairrada, Vinho Verde, Alentejo). Both rows point to the same parent entity (Niepoort since 1842), but Projectos carries a distinct brand identity on its labels (§11.2). Producer B (Niepoort) is parent; Producer A (Niepoort Projectos) is child.

Web evidence reveals two distinct Rothschild wine enterprises under shared family ownership. 'Baron Philippe de Rothschild' (BPDR, bpdr.com) produces blended wines from Bordeaux appellations — matching Producer B's portfolio (Pauillac, Bordeaux, Médoc, Sauternes, Champagne, Corbières). 'Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite)' (lafite.com) is the separate Lafite-Rothschild estate group. Producer A ('Baron de Rothschild', singular) carries only Languedoc/Corbières/Pays d'Oc wines with the 'Aussieres' line, suggesting a distinct sub-brand or regional bottling line. The shared 'Aussieres' wine and TTB permittee diversity on B (13 different individuals, typical of a brand distributed through multiple importers) indicate B is the primary 'Barons de Rothschild' brand. Producer A appears to be a regional or secondary label under the same Rothschild corporate umbrella — distinct label identity ('Baron' singular vs 'Barons' plural) but controlled by the same family enterprise. §11.2 PARENT-CHILD applies: distinct brand identities on labels, shared ownership.

Web evidence reveals Pascal Marchand is the founder/operator behind both entities. Search result [B1] states 'Pascal Marchand, a Quebecker, came to Burgundy in 1983...In 2006, he became a micro-negociant.' Search result [A2] confirms 'the extraordinary story of Pascal Marchand, the French Canadian boy wonder, who in 1985...became winemaker at Domaine Comte Armand' and later founded Marchand-Tawse. The two producer rows represent distinct brand identities on labels ('Marchand-Tawse' vs 'Pascal Marchand'), with overlapping wine catalogs (shared vineyard names: Les Suchots, Les Faconnieres, Les Cazetiers, Clos des Ormes, Les Feusselottes, Aux Boudots, Les Damodes, Cailleret, Les Vaucrains). Per §11.2 and §11.4.f, this is a négociant + personal-brand pattern under single ownership — Pascal Marchand (domaine/personal brand) is the parent; Marchand-Tawse (négociant partnership entity) is the child. Shared TTB permittees (BERNADETTE LEGGIERO, BRIAN LEVY, PHILIP BURKHART) further confirm operational linkage.

Web evidence reveals Pascal Marchand (Burgundy micro-négociant since 2006) co-founded Marchand & Burch with Jeff Burch, uniting Burgundy and Western Australian terroirs. Marchand & Burch is a distinct brand partnership/label under Pascal Marchand's portfolio, not a separate producer. The 3-wine Marchand & Burch catalog (all Grand Cru Burgundy) is a curated subset of Pascal Marchand's broader 50-wine négociant business. Per §11.2 and §11.4.l, this is PARENT_CHILD: Pascal Marchand (parent/négociant) → Marchand & Burch (child/partnership brand with distinct label identity).

Web evidence reveals a continuous Gaunoux family winemaking lineage: Henri Gaunoux (celebrated vigneron mid-20th century) → Jean-Michel Gaunoux (established his own domaine in 1990) → Henri Gaunoux (Jean-Michel's son, current winemaker). Michel Gaunoux appears as a separate branch or predecessor entity (Domaine Michel Gaunoux founded 1875). The wine catalogs show partial overlap (both produce Meursault, Corton, Volnay) but distinct primary focuses (Michel: Pommard-centric; Jean-Michel: Puligny-Montrachet/Meursault-centric), consistent with related but operationally distinct domaines under the same family umbrella. Per §11.2, this is PARENT-CHILD rather than MERGE — distinct brand identities on labels ('Michel Gaunoux' vs 'Jean-Michel Gaunoux') with documented family ownership continuity.

Both producers share TTB permit BW-CA-5756 but display distinct brand identities on labels (SANDLANDS vs COULOIR). Web evidence confirms separate winemakers with different philosophies: Sandlands is Tegan Passalacqua's project focused on forgotten California varieties; Couloir is Grant's mountain-themed Pinot Noir specialist. §11.2 applies — same licensed facility (Walter Richardson permittee), distinct brands. Couloir appears to be a second label or sister brand under the same BW permit, making this PARENT_CHILD rather than MERGE.

Web evidence reveals both Substance and CasaSmith are brands under the same corporate umbrella: House of Smith (Charles Smith's portfolio). Substance Wines was founded by Charles Smith and later acquired by O'Neill Vintners & Distillers; CasaSmith joined House of Smith in 2012 as a distinct brand focusing on Italian varietals. Both share BW-WA-336 permit (custom-crush or shared facility pattern per §11.4.j), but maintain separate brand identities on labels and distinct wine catalogs (Substance: Cabernet/Merlot/Sauvignon Blanc; CasaSmith: Sangiovese/Barbera/Italian focus). This is a sister-winery / portfolio relationship: same permittee entity, different consumer-facing brands. PARENT_CHILD with House of Smith / O'Neill as parent.

Web evidence reveals that Domaine Emilian Gillet is a distinct brand created in 1998 by Jean Thévenet to honor an ancestral winemaker, while Domaine Guillemot-Michel is a separate family estate in Quintaine. Both produce the same rare 'Quintaine' cuvée from Viré-Clessé (shared wine signal), but they are independent producers with different legal identities and ownership. The Thévenet family connection and the deliberate naming of Emilian Gillet as a heritage cuvée suggest Emilian Gillet may be a secondary/heritage label under Thévenet family stewardship rather than a full merger. However, the distinct brand identities on labels, separate websites, and independent producer registrations (per Jancis Robinson and Infinivin) indicate they should remain separate rows linked by parent-child relationship if there is documented family/ownership overlap, or SKIP if they are truly independent. Given the web evidence points to Thévenet family ownership of Emilian Gillet and Guillemot-Michel's independent family operation, and both maintain distinct brand identities on their labels, this is best classified as PARENT_CHILD with Thévenet/Bongran as potential parent, or SKIP if no direct ownership link exists. Confidence lowered slightly due to ambiguity in the exact ownership structure from web snippets alone.

Web evidence reveals that 'L'Esprit Destieu' and 'Grand Destieu' are distinct wines from the same château (Château Grand Destieu), not separate producers. Vivino and Vinous both list 'Grand Destieu L'Esprit Destieu' as a secondary wine of Château Grand Destieu (the flagship). Per §11.4.e, second wines are wines, not producers — but the staging import created 'Esprit Destieu' as a separate producer row. The correct model is: Château Grand Destieu (parent producer) → L'Esprit Destieu (secondary wine). Producer B ('Grand Destieu') is the correct primary producer; Producer A should be soft-deleted and its wine re-linked to B as a secondary wine of Grand Destieu.

Web evidence (idealwine.com result [1]) explicitly states 'Château de Plince's second wine is dark ruby in colour...' — identifying La Fleur de Plince as the second wine of Château de Plince. Per §11.4.e, second wines are wines of the parent producer, not separate producers. However, both rows exist as distinct producer entries in the database. The correct model is PARENT_CHILD: Château de Plince (parent, likely missing from current rows or conflated) with La Fleur de Plince as the child/second label. Given the data structure, classify as PARENT_CHILD with La Fleur de Plince as child, pending clarification of whether a primary Château de Plince row exists separately.

Web evidence reveals a family structure: Jean-Louis Dutraive is the founding producer (pioneer of organic/natural winemaking in Fleurie per Wine Scholar Guild); his son Justin Dutraive launched a separate label 'Domaine de la Grand'Cour' in 2015 (per The Source Imports). Producer A 'Dutraive' appears to be a short-form brand name used by Jean-Louis Dutraive's operation (Polaner Selections lists 'Dutraive, Famille'), while Producer B 'Jean-Louis Dutraive' is the full/official name. However, the web also indicates Justin Dutraive as a distinct producer with his own label. The catalog overlap (Chenas, Lantignie, Fleurie crus) and substring containment suggest A is a variant of B's brand, but the family-business structure and Justin's separate 2015 launch indicate potential PARENT_CHILD rather than simple MERGE. Given thin data (no TTB, no external IDs, only 4 wines total), treat as PARENT_CHILD with Jean-Louis Dutraive as parent and 'Dutraive' (short form) as a secondary brand under the same entity, pending clarification of whether 'Dutraive' is a distinct label or a house variant.

Web evidence reveals that 'Fonseca & Van Zeller' is a joint venture between José Maria da Fonseca (major Portuguese producer) and Cristiano van Zeller, while 'Van Zellers & Co' is the independent Van Zeller family estate with continuous Douro heritage since 1620. These are distinct brand identities on labels (one is a partnership, one is a family name), but they share ownership/control via the Van Zeller family member. Per §11.2, this is PARENT_CHILD: Van Zellers & Co (parent, the independent family estate) and Fonseca & Van Zeller (child, the JV partnership). The two wines confirm separate product lines — Vintage Port (JV) vs. Iron Maiden Douro red (family estate).

Web evidence clarifies the relationship: Rolf Binder is the primary winery (established 1955, rolfbinder.com official site), while Binder Mitchell is a distinct brand partnership between Rolf Binder and Kevin Mitchell (CellarTracker: 'made by Rolf Binder & Kevin Mitchell'). The parenthetical in Producer A's name ('Rolf Binder (Binder Mitchell)') indicates an alternate/secondary brand under the same entity, not a synonym. Per §11.2, this is a portfolio/secondary-label pattern: Rolf Binder Wines is the parent producer; Binder Mitchell is a child brand (joint venture or secondary label). The two rows should not MERGE but should be linked via parent_producer_id, with 'Rolf Binder' as parent.

Web evidence reveals both producers are part of 'Les Vignobles de Larose' (Responsible Vineyards group). The History page explicitly states 'Trintaudon and Perganson wines were once more in production' under the same umbrella. Château Larose (Saint-Émilion) and Château Larose-Perganson (Haut-Médoc) are distinct brand identities on their respective labels but share corporate ownership via the Vignobles de Larose holding company. This is a classic portfolio structure (§11.2): same parent entity, different appellations, different label brands. Producer A (Larose) is the parent/umbrella; Producer B (Larose Perganson) is a distinct child brand within the group.
